set.notes: UPDATED 2026-11-18 (research batch 8): RESOLVED (negative). The NSW Data Centre Guidelines define the term: 'Recycled water includes that provided by recycled water networks or on-site water treatment, such as from captured stormwater.' Read against all 20 archived consent instruments and the modification reports read in batch 7, no consent or modification cites that definition or relies on it to meet a recycled-water expectation. Only two assessment reports mention the Guidelines (Glendenning Road and Project Apollo, both after their release on 17 August 2026); each says 'The Department has considered the Guidelines as a relevant consideration under section 4.15 of the EP&A Act' and lists the related conditions as renewable power purchase, retrofit capability, PUE and WUE monitoring through a Sustainability Management Plan, and amenity; recycled water is not among them. The closest usage predates the Guidelines: the DigiCo SYD1 consent (December 2025) lists, under 'Recycled water and reuse, through:', the 'Use of 2x5000L existing rainwater tanks', rainwater counted as recycled water, which is the reading the later definition allows. The three consents decided since July 2026 (Project Pluto, Project Apollo, Glendenning Road) instead require a 'review of available water servicing arrangements, in consultation with the relevant water service provider, to identify any alternative non-potable or recycled water supply options'. Re-open if a Sustainability Management Plan approved under one of them relies on the definition.

set.notes: ANSWERED 2026-11-15 for the renewable-energy obligation; the hypothesis is FALSIFIED. The 'no ratchet' finding does not hold. Three of the 20 archived consent instruments (19 distinct projects - Davis Road appears twice, original and MOD 1) obligate the Applicant, before operation may commence and to the Planning Secretary's satisfaction, to offset all GHG from electricity 'including both non-IT and IT loads' by matching all operational demand to 'a portfolio of additional, firmed renewable energy supply at all times', with a Power Purchase Agreement and firming agreement for NSW-based supply within the NEM and a shortfall framework: Project Pluto SSD-69223466 B19/B20 (determined 23 July 2026), Project Apollo SSD-74069708 B22/B23 (2 September 2026), Glendenning Road SSD-73761707 B20/B21/B22/B23 (instrument dated 14 September 2026; the portal's determination field reads 16 September). None of the 16 earlier determinations in the archive carries it. In each case the Department's assessment report records a materially weaker offer first and then recommends the condition anyway: Glendenning p55 offered '100% renewable energy by 2040' against p56's pre-operation obligation; Apollo p59 said it 'has been purchasing 100% renewable electricity for electricity under their operational control' and the Department held outcomes 'materially dependent on the successful securing and performance of renewable energy procurement'; Pluto's EPA advice (p27) went no further than 'purchasing of renewable energy certificates', while its ESD Report (p50) offered 500 kW of rooftop solar offsetting 658 MWh/yr and 540 t CO2-e against 467,924 t CO2-e/yr stated - about 0.12% by arithmetic on the report's own two figures, a derivation and not a quoted fact. WHAT IS NOT RATCHETED: the numeric targets stay proponent-set (PUE 1.17 Glendenning, 1.4 Pluto); the conditions require reporting against them, not achieving a Department number. The ratchet is on timing, additionality, firming, geography and auditing - Glendenning B22 adds continuous IT-vs-total metering, annual PUE/WUE/CO2-e reporting, alignment with the NSW Guide for Large Emitters (EPA, 2025), prioritising recycled or non-potable water where available, and three-yearly revision, and B23 bars operation until the plan is approved. TIMING IS NARROWER THAN '2026': 1-5 Khartoum Road SSD-63235720, determined 11 March 2026, has renewable and PUE language and no at-all-times obligation, so the change falls between 11 March and 23 July 2026. CORRECTIONS to this gap's earlier note, which was written against 18 instruments: 20 instruments for 19 projects; EIGHT consents mention renewable supply (not four) and SEVEN mention PUE (not five). STILL OPEN, so this gap stays in_progress: no EIS is archived for any determined project, so the other 16 comparisons run through the assessment report's summary of the ESD Report; air quality, noise, water and traffic conditions are untested for a ratchet; the three firmed consents are also the three largest recent approvals, so 'the Department ratchets' and 'it ratchets on the biggest projects' cannot be separated; and Lanceley Place Artarmon SSD-66777221, approved 11 April 2025, has no instrument in the archive and no assessment-report attachment on its portal record, so the scan cannot speak to it. The policy text the conditions refer to ('in accordance with applicable NSW government policy') has not been located, so the cause of the mid-2026 change is not established. Full chain with page cites and SHA-256 prefixes: reports/hunts/RG-061.md. UPDATED 2026-11-18 (research batch 8): GENERATOR HOURS AND DIESEL, counted by this pack's script across the 20 archived consent instruments (18 data centre consents; the Davis Road Mod 1 instrument and the Dicker Data warehouse carry no generator cap). 15 cap generator operation at 200 hours a year; the three decided since July 2026 set lower caps: Project Pluto 'exceed 173 hours per year', Project Apollo 187 and Glendenning Road 170. Project Apollo's cap is the applicant's own figure, not a tightening: its report says 'Routine generator testing of up to 187 hours per year is required', and that 'In response to EPA advice' the applicant said 'the generator operating regime has been revised to remain below 200 hours per year'. 200 hours is the line in the Guidelines: 'Current regulations allow data centres to use generators for up to 200 hours a year without being subject to any point source emission limits for oxides of nitrogen'. The EPA's own reason for the cap is on the record at Macquarie Park: 'To ensure an EPL is not required, the EPA recommended a condition be imposed restricting the use and/or testing of any back-up generators installed at the site to a maximum of 200 hours per year.' At 1-5 Khartoum Road the consent condition is 200 hours while its own mitigation table says 'Total generator testing time is limited to 72 hours per year': the condition does not lock in the offer. 13 of the instruments say diesel storage 'does not exceed 2,000 tonnes', the licensing line for petroleum storage (RG-008). So on generator hours there is no ratchet below the 200-hour line except in the three newest consents, and in one of those the cap is exactly the applicant's offer.

set.notes: Peer review confirmed to EXIST and to be rare (~5% of projects). Reviewing firms are not named in the filenames. Three documents to open. UPDATED 2026-11-18 (research batch 8): RESOLVED for the documents on the public record. Six of the 63 projects in the attachment index carry a review document by title: two acoustic peer reviews (DigiCo SYD1; Lane Cove West Mod 3); an acoustic and an air quality 'review statement' on 51 Huntingwood Drive Mod 1, a withdrawn modification (the acoustic one answered 401, not public; refusal recorded); and three greenhouse gas reviews (Project Atlas; Roberts Road Mods 2 and 4). OPENED: at DigiCo SYD1, 'Renzo Tonin & Associates (RTA) was engaged by Patch Planning, on behalf of HDI SYD1 Property Holdings Pty Limited (DigiCo) to peer review the noise and vibration impact assessment (NVIA) report undertaken by Pulse White Noise Acoustics (PWNA)', across 'reviews or partial reviews of eight revisions'. At Lane Cove West Mod 3 the same reviewer 'was engaged by EMKC Cubed Management (EMKC) to undertake an independent review of the Noise Impact Assessment (NIA) prepared by Pulse White Noise Acoustics (PWNA)', in 'seven reviews of the NIA'. Both letters say 'The peer review process did not involve any detailed modelling checks or remodelling by RTA.' At Roberts Road Mod 4, 'Zephyr Environmental Pty Ltd (Zephyr) has been engaged by Canberra Data Centres (CDC) to perform an independent review' of SLR Consulting's greenhouse gas report ('Revision 05, SLR Consulting, 16 July 2026'); under the EPA's Guide for Large Emitters, above 100,000 tonnes a year 'mitigation assessments must be verified by an independent expert review'. All three greenhouse reviews are by the same firm, Zephyr Environmental: Roberts Road Mod 2 ('engaged by Urbis, on behalf of Canberra Data Centres (CDC)', reviewing SLR's report) and Project Atlas, where 'The Assessment Report has been prepared by LCI on behalf of Goodman Property Services' and the reviewer 'has been engaged by LCI Consultants (LCI ), on behalf of Goodman Property Services': there the author of the report engaged its reviewer. The Mod 2 and Atlas letters each say 'No actual or perceived conflicts of interest have come to my attention, and I have not been employed by the proponent within the last five years'; the Mod 4 letter, written after the Mod 2 engagement for the same proponent, carries no such statement. Each review found the work 'adequate' or 'satisfactory'. ANSWER: in every review opened the reviewer is a different firm from the author, so no firm was found reviewing its own work; every review was engaged by the applicant, its planner or the report's author, none by the Department; the acoustic reviews checked by comment and meeting, not by re-running the model. The greenhouse reviews follow the EPA's rule; nothing read requires the acoustic ones.
